passages.title: Why we put things off
passages.text: Most of us procrastinate from time to time, but some people do so to such an extent that it affects their health and careers. For a long time, procrastination was put down to laziness or poor time management. Recent research, however, suggests that it has more to do with emotions than with organization. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or insecure, delaying it brings immediate relief, even though it creates more stress later. This may account for the fact that people with low self-esteem are particularly likely to procrastinate: every task becomes a test they are afraid of failing. Psychologists therefore tend to play down the importance of productivity apps and detailed schedules. What they recommend instead is learning to tolerate uncomfortable feelings. Breaking a task into very small steps, forgiving yourself for past delays and weighing the real cost of waiting can all bring about lasting change. Interestingly, people who are kinder to themselves after a failure appear to procrastinate less, not more. Self-criticism, it seems, does not motivate us; it simply makes the task feel even more threatening.

passages.title: Habits and the comfort zone
passages.text: What keeps most of us in our comfort zone is not laziness but the brain's preference for the familiar. Routines save energy: once a behavior has become second nature, we no longer need to think about it. The problem is that the same mechanism makes change difficult. It is only when we repeat a new behavior many times that it starts to feel automatic, and the first weeks are usually the hardest. Social factors also play a part. Teenagers are often warned about peer pressure, but adults are just as influenced by the people around them, whether they realize it or not. If your friends exercise regularly, you are far more likely to do the same. Psychologists describe people who cope well with setbacks as resilient. Contrary to popular belief, resilience is not a fixed personality trait. It is a set of skills, such as asking for help and seeing failure as temporary, that can be learned at any age. What resilient people seem to share is not an absence of fear, but a willingness to act in spite of it.

points: Estos phrasal verbs hablan de causas y decisiones, y son comunes en textos de análisis.
«account for» es explicar o ser la causa: «Stress may account for these symptoms».
«bring about» es provocar un cambio; «weigh up», sopesar; «play down», restar importancia.
Los separables llevan el pronombre en medio: «play it down», «weigh them up».
